Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

For bounded $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, in the metric sense of [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], its **Jordan outer content** is the infimum of $\sum_{r<q}\operatorname{vol}(R_r)$ over finite axis-parallel rectangle covers of $E$. Its **Jordan inner content** is the supremum of the same sums over finite families of rectangles contained in $E$ whose interiors are pairwise disjoint.

Metric boundedness always supplies a nondegenerate bounding rectangle. For
nonempty $E$, choose $x_0\in\mathbb R^m$ and $r>0$ with
$E\subseteq B(x_0,r)$. Since
$|x_j-(x_0)_j|\le d_\infty(x,x_0)\le d_2(x,x_0)<r$ for every coordinate
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] clause 3, [[def-metric-ball]]), the nondegenerate box
$\prod_{j<m}[(x_0)_j-r,(x_0)_j+r]$ contains $E$. The empty set lies in
any fixed nondegenerate rectangle.

Thus the outer family is nonempty and the same bounding rectangle bounds the
inner sums; the empty family gives inner sum $0$. Refining all listed
endpoints into one grid and splitting the nested finite sums shows every
inscribed sum is at most every covering sum
([[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).
Completeness therefore supplies finite real extrema
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]],
[[lem-sup-unique]]).

The set is **Jordan measurable** when the contents agree, and their common value is its **Jordan content**. The empty set and every degenerate rectangle have content $0$.

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its boundary $\partial E$ is null, equivalently has content zero.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.
A bounded real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable if and only if its discontinuity set is null.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

derivations.claim: The box $Q$ is closed and bounded because it is a finite product of closed bounded intervals; [F3] therefore makes $Q$ compact. Its boundary is the union of the $2m$ coordinate faces $F_{r,-}:=\{x\in Q:x_r=a_r\}$ and $F_{r,+}:=\{x\in Q:x_r=b_r\}$, since a point of $Q$ is interior exactly when all its coordinates lie strictly between the endpoints.

For $r=1,\ldots,m$ put $C_r:=\prod_{j\ne r}(b_j-a_j+2)$, with the empty product $1$, and let $C:=\max(1,C_1,\ldots,C_m)$. Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and choose $0<\delta<\min(1,\varepsilon/(4mC))$. Each face $F_{r,\pm}$ is covered by the rectangle that thickens its fixed $r$-coordinate by $\delta$ and enlarges every other interval by $\delta$. By [F1], this cover has volume $$2\delta\prod_{j\ne r}(b_j-a_j+2\delta)\le2\delta C <\varepsilon/(2m).$$ Thus each face has zero outer content by [F2]. The finite union of the $2m$ faces has content zero: the displayed covers have total volume less than $\varepsilon$. Since their union is $\partial Q$ by step 1.1, the boundary has content zero.

The box is bounded and has boundary of content zero by step 2.1, so [F4] makes $Q$ Jordan measurable. For any stated endpoint variant $R$, its boundary is contained in the same coordinate faces from step 1.1, hence has content zero by step 2.1; since $R$ is bounded, [F4] makes it Jordan measurable as well.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. By [F5], $f$ is Riemann integrable on $Q$ and therefore bounded there. For any endpoint variant $R$, extend $f|_R$ by zero to $Q$. At every point outside $\partial R$ this extension is either $f$ on a neighborhood in $R$ or zero on a neighborhood in $Q\setminus \overline R$; thus its discontinuities lie in $\partial R$. The boundary has content zero by step 3.1, hence is null by [F2]. Then [F6] makes this zero extension integrable on $Q$, and [F7] gives the Riemann integrability of $f|_R$ over $R$.

For $m\ge2$, a closed coordinate face of $Q$ is a closed rectangle in $\mathbb R^{m-1}$, so it is compact by [F3]. Applying steps 1.1–4.1 in dimension $m-1$ proves its Jordan measurability and the stated integrability of every endpoint variant on that face.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), let $(U,x)$ be a
smooth chart, and define the local **metric density** by
$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}$ on $U$, using the matrix of metric components
in this chart. This definition requires no orientation or volume form. Write
$g^{ab}$ for the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]) and
$\Gamma^{a}{}_{bc}$ for the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in the chart.

**(a) Derivative of the density.** At every point of $U$,

$$\partial_a w=\tfrac12\,w\,g^{bc}\,\partial_a g_{bc}.$$

**(b) Trace of the Christoffel symbols.** At every point of $U$,

$$\Gamma^{b}{}_{ba}=w^{-1}\partial_a w .$$

**(c) Divergence formula.** For every smooth vector field $J$ on $M$, at every
point of $U$,

$$\nabla_aJ^a=\partial_aJ^a+\Gamma^{a}{}_{ab}J^b=w^{-1}\partial_a\bigl(w\,J^a\bigr),$$

where $\nabla_aJ^a=g^{ab}\nabla_bJ_a$ is the divergence of $J$ contracted with
the metric and $J^a$ are the components of $J$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).

The identity of (c) is a chart formula for a chart-independent scalar: the
right-hand side is independent of the chart, as the left-hand side is.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Since $J$ is $C^1$, [F2] gives $\nabla_aJ^a=\partial_aJ^a+\Gamma^a{}_{ab}J^b$. Multiplying by $w$ and substituting step 1.1 yields $$w\nabla_aJ^a=w\partial_aJ^a+(\partial_aw)J^a=\partial_a(wJ^a),$$ by the product rule for $C^1$ functions. Dividing by $w>0$ proves the stated identity.

$(-,+,+,+)$ and an independent orientation, with the exact meanings in
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The tangent-bundle smooth
structure follows the stated Countable Choice convention
[[def-countable-choice]]. Let $(U,x)$ be a positively oriented chart with
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ and $x(U)=V\subseteq\mathbb R^4$. Coordinates here are
mathematical real coordinates; no physical units are assigned.

Choose real numbers $t_0<t_1$ and $a_i<b_i$ for $i=1,2,3$, and let
$$\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(a_i,b_i),\qquad \overline\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3[a_i,b_i],\qquad K=[t_0,t_1]\times\Omega,\qquad \overline K=[t_0,t_1]\times\overline\Omega\subset V.$$
The finite integration slab $K$ is a bounded Jordan set and its closure
$\overline K$ is a compact coordinate box. Assume $\overline K$ has an open
neighborhood in $V$ on which the spatial metric block
$h_{ij}:=g_{ij}$ is positive definite and the inverse-metric component
$g^{00}$ is negative. Thus each slice
$\Sigma_t=\{x^{-1}(t,x^1,x^2,x^3):(x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\Omega\}$ is spacelike.
Assume also that the future unit normal defined below is future-directed in the
given time orientation. The closure $\overline K$, its closed coordinate
faces, the open spatial rectangle $\Omega$, the mixed-endpoint slab $K$, and
the corresponding mixed-endpoint side-face rectangles are Jordan sets by
[[lem-tgr-coordinate-boxes-are-compact-jordan]].

Write $g^{ab}$ for the inverse matrix to $g_{ab}$ and put
$$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|},\qquad \alpha:=(-g^{00})^{-1/2},\qquad n^a:=-\alpha g^{a0},\qquad n_a:=-\alpha\,\delta_a^0.$$
Then $n$ is the future unit normal to every $\Sigma_t$; its unit and normal
properties follow from $g^{ab}n_an_b=-1$ and
$g_{ab}n^b=n_a$. Let $dV_h:=\sqrt{\det(h_{ij})}\,dx^1dx^2dx^3$ be the
Riemannian volume element of the induced positive-definite slice metric.
In this positively oriented chart the metric volume form is
$\mathrm{vol}_g=w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$ by
[[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (a).

A **current** here is a $C^1$ vector field $J=J^a\partial_a$ on an open
neighborhood of $x^{-1}(\overline K)$; equivalently, its coordinate components $J^a$
are $C^1$. Its current three-form is the pointwise contraction
$\omega_J:=\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$, where
$(\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g)(X_1,X_2,X_3):=
\mathrm{vol}_g(J,X_1,X_2,X_3)$. In coordinates,
$$\omega_J=w\bigl(J^0dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3 -J^1dx^0\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3 +J^2dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^3 -J^3dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\bigr).$$
The slice orientation is chosen so that the future unit normal precedes a
positive slice basis. Since $n^0=1/\alpha>0$ and the spacetime chart is
positive, this slice orientation is $dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$; the
pullback of $\omega_J$ to $\Sigma_t$ is $wJ^0dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.
Define its signed **slice charge** (the normal flux through the spacelike
slice) by
$$Q_J(t):=\int_\Omega -g(J,n)\,dV_h.$$
Every displayed integral is the Riemann integral over the indicated bounded
Jordan set, as defined in
[[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]. The current and metric extend
continuously to the compact coordinate closure, and
[[lem-tgr-coordinate-boxes-are-compact-jordan]] proves that the open spatial
and mixed-endpoint rectangles are Jordan measurable and that these continuous
densities are Riemann integrable there.

Let $B$ denote the union of the six side faces of $K$, with outward boundary
orientation; each face is integrated over its relative interior, a bounded
Jordan rectangle whose closure is compact. The upper $x^i$ face has induced orientation
$(-1)^i dx^0\wedge\cdots\widehat{dx^i}\cdots\wedge dx^3$; the lower face
has its opposite. Thus the $i$th current-three-form pullback integrates to
the upper-minus-lower $wJ^i$ coordinate expression below. Define the
**net outward side flux** $\Phi_J(B)$ as the sum over
the three spatial coordinate directions of upper-face flux minus lower-face
flux. More explicitly, for $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ let $\Omega_i$ be the product
Jordan rectangle in the three coordinates other than $x^i$, with endpoint
convention $x^0\in[t_0,t_1]$ and $x^j\in(a_j,b_j)$ for $j\ne i$; then
$$\Phi_J(B):=\sum_{i=1}^3\int_{\Omega_i} \left. wJ^i\right|_{x^i=b_i}-\left. wJ^i\right|_{x^i=a_i}\,d^3x_{\widehat i}.$$
The integrals use the standard increasing-coordinate order on each face. For
a $C^1$ current the three-form coefficients are continuous, so the displayed
rectangular integrals exist. This extends the smooth-current flux convention
of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (b) to the present
finite coordinate faces. No unit normal to a side face is part of this
definition; in particular the flux form remains defined if a side face is
null. The term “charge” names this mathematical flux integral only; it does
not assert a physical conservation law or an entropy interpretation.

Riemannian volume element of the induced positive-definite slice metric.
In this positively oriented chart the metric volume form is
$\mathrm{vol}_g=w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$ by
[[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (a).

A **current** here is a $C^1$ vector field $J=J^a\partial_a$ on an open
neighborhood of $x^{-1}(\overline K)$; equivalently, its coordinate components $J^a$
are $C^1$. Its current three-form is the pointwise contraction
$\omega_J:=\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$, where
$(\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g)(X_1,X_2,X_3):=
\mathrm{vol}_g(J,X_1,X_2,X_3)$. In coordinates,
$$\omega_J=w\bigl(J^0dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3 -J^1dx^0\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3 +J^2dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^3 -J^3dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\bigr).$$
The slice orientation is chosen so that the future unit normal precedes a
positive slice basis. Since $n^0=1/\alpha>0$ and the spacetime chart is
positive, this slice orientation is $dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$; the
pullback of $\omega_J$ to $\Sigma_t$ is $wJ^0dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.
Define its signed **slice charge** (the normal flux through the spacelike
slice) by
$$Q_J(t):=\int_\Omega -g(J,n)\,dV_h.$$
Every displayed integral is the Riemann integral over the indicated bounded
Jordan set, as defined in
[[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]. The current and metric extend
continuously to the compact coordinate closure, and
[[lem-tgr-coordinate-boxes-are-compact-jordan]] proves that the open spatial
and mixed-endpoint rectangles are Jordan measurable and that these continuous
densities are Riemann integrable there.

Let $B$ denote the union of the six side faces of $K$, with outward boundary
orientation; each face is integrated over its relative interior, a bounded
Jordan rectangle whose closure is compact. The upper $x^i$ face has induced orientation
$(-1)^i dx^0\wedge\cdots\widehat{dx^i}\cdots\wedge dx^3$; the lower face
has its opposite. Thus the $i$th current-three-form pullback integrates to
the upper-minus-lower $wJ^i$ coordinate expression below. Define the
**net outward side flux** $\Phi_J(B)$ as the sum over
the three spatial coordinate directions of upper-face flux minus lower-face
flux. More explicitly, for $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ let $\Omega_i$ be the product
Jordan rectangle in the three coordinates other than $x^i$, with endpoint
convention $x^0\in[t_0,t_1]$ and $x^j\in(a_j,b_j)$ for $j\ne i$; then
$$\Phi_J(B):=\sum_{i=1}^3\int_{\Omega_i} \left. wJ^i\right|_{x^i=b_i}-\left. wJ^i\right|_{x^i=a_i}\,d^3x_{\widehat i}.$$
The integrals use the standard increasing-coordinate order on each face. For
a $C^1$ current the three-form coefficients are continuous, so the displayed
rectangular integrals exist. This extends the smooth-current flux convention
of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (b) to the present
finite coordinate faces. No unit normal to a side face is part of this
definition; in particular the flux form remains defined if a side face is
null. The term “charge” names this mathematical flux integral only; it does
not assert a physical conservation law or an entropy interpretation.

derivations.claim: In the coordinate basis write the metric matrix as $$G=\begin{pmatrix}g_{00}&b^{\mathsf T}\\ b&h\end{pmatrix},$$ where $b_i=g_{i0}$. Since $h$ is positive definite it is invertible. Subtract $b^{\mathsf T}h^{-1}$ times the lower block rows from the first row; this determinant-preserving operation gives $$\det G=\det(h)\,S,\qquad S:=g_{00}-b^{\mathsf T}h^{-1}b.$$ To identify the inverse entry, solve $Gz=e_0$: the lower equations give $z_{\rm sp}=-h^{-1}bz_0$, and the first equation then gives $Sz_0=1$. Therefore $g^{00}=z_0=S^{-1}$, so $S<0$ by [F1].
From $S=(g^{00})^{-1}<0$ and the definition of $\alpha$, $\alpha=\sqrt{-S}$. As $\det h>0$, step 1.1 yields $$w=\sqrt{|\det G|}=\sqrt{\det h}\sqrt{-S} =\alpha\sqrt{\det h}.$$

Lowering the index of $n$ gives $n_a=-\alpha\delta_a^0$ by [F1], hence $-g(J,n)=-J^an_a=\alpha J^0$. Substitute step 2.1 into the defining integrand of $Q_J(t)$ to obtain $$-g(J,n)\sqrt{\det h}=\alpha J^0\sqrt{\det h}=wJ^0.$$ Integrating over $\Omega$ proves the statement.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Use a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ and an independent orientation, with the exact meanings in
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The tangent-bundle smooth
structure follows the stated Countable Choice convention
[[def-countable-choice]]. Let $(U,x)$ be a positively oriented chart with
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ and $x(U)=V\subseteq\mathbb R^4$. Coordinates here are
mathematical real coordinates; no physical units are assigned.

Choose real numbers $t_0<t_1$ and $a_i<b_i$ for $i=1,2,3$, and let
$$\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(a_i,b_i),\qquad \overline\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3[a_i,b_i],\qquad K=[t_0,t_1]\times\Omega,\qquad \overline K=[t_0,t_1]\times\overline\Omega\subset V.$$
The finite integration slab $K$ is a bounded Jordan set and its closure
$\overline K$ is a compact coordinate box. Assume $\overline K$ has an open
neighborhood in $V$ on which the spatial metric block
$h_{ij}:=g_{ij}$ is positive definite and the inverse-metric component
$g^{00}$ is negative. Thus each slice
$\Sigma_t=\{x^{-1}(t,x^1,x^2,x^3):(x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\Omega\}$ is spacelike.
Assume also that the future unit normal defined below is future-directed in the
given time orientation. The closure $\overline K$, its closed coordinate
faces, the open spatial rectangle $\Omega$, the mixed-endpoint slab $K$, and
the corresponding mixed-endpoint side-face rectangles are Jordan sets by
[[lem-tgr-coordinate-boxes-are-compact-jordan]].

Write $g^{ab}$ for the inverse matrix to $g_{ab}$ and put
$$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|},\qquad \alpha:=(-g^{00})^{-1/2},\qquad n^a:=-\alpha g^{a0},\qquad n_a:=-\alpha\,\delta_a^0.$$
Then $n$ is the future unit normal to every $\Sigma_t$; its unit and normal
properties follow from $g^{ab}n_an_b=-1$ and
$g_{ab}n^b=n_a$. Let $dV_h:=\sqrt{\det(h_{ij})}\,dx^1dx^2dx^3$ be the
Riemannian volume element of the induced positive-definite slice metric.
In this positively oriented chart the metric volume form is
$\mathrm{vol}_g=w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$ by
[[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (a).

A **current** here is a $C^1$ vector field $J=J^a\partial_a$ on an open
neighborhood of $x^{-1}(\overline K)$; equivalently, its coordinate components $J^a$
are $C^1$. Its current three-form is the pointwise contraction
$\omega_J:=\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$, where
$(\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g)(X_1,X_2,X_3):=
\mathrm{vol}_g(J,X_1,X_2,X_3)$. In coordinates,
$$\omega_J=w\bigl(J^0dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3 -J^1dx^0\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3 +J^2dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^3 -J^3dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\bigr).$$
The slice orientation is chosen so that the future unit normal precedes a
positive slice basis. Since $n^0=1/\alpha>0$ and the spacetime chart is
positive, this slice orientation is $dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$; the
pullback of $\omega_J$ to $\Sigma_t$ is $wJ^0dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.
Define its signed **slice charge** (the normal flux through the spacelike
slice) by
$$Q_J(t):=\int_\Omega -g(J,n)\,dV_h.$$
Every displayed integral is the Riemann integral over the indicated bounded
Jordan set, as defined in
[[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]. The current and metric extend
continuously to the compact coordinate closure, and
[[lem-tgr-coordinate-boxes-are-compact-jordan]] proves that the open spatial
and mixed-endpoint rectangles are Jordan measurable and that these continuous
densities are Riemann integrable there.

Let $B$ denote the union of the six side faces of $K$, with outward boundary
orientation; each face is integrated over its relative interior, a bounded
Jordan rectangle whose closure is compact. The upper $x^i$ face has induced orientation
$(-1)^i dx^0\wedge\cdots\widehat{dx^i}\cdots\wedge dx^3$; the lower face
has its opposite. Thus the $i$th current-three-form pullback integrates to
the upper-minus-lower $wJ^i$ coordinate expression below. Define the
**net outward side flux** $\Phi_J(B)$ as the sum over
the three spatial coordinate directions of upper-face flux minus lower-face
flux. More explicitly, for $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ let $\Omega_i$ be the product
Jordan rectangle in the three coordinates other than $x^i$, with endpoint
convention $x^0\in[t_0,t_1]$ and $x^j\in(a_j,b_j)$ for $j\ne i$; then
$$\Phi_J(B):=\sum_{i=1}^3\int_{\Omega_i} \left. wJ^i\right|_{x^i=b_i}-\left. wJ^i\right|_{x^i=a_i}\,d^3x_{\widehat i}.$$
The integrals use the standard increasing-coordinate order on each face. For
a $C^1$ current the three-form coefficients are continuous, so the displayed
rectangular integrals exist. This extends the smooth-current flux convention
of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (b) to the present
finite coordinate faces. No unit normal to a side face is part of this
definition; in particular the flux form remains defined if a side face is
null. The term “charge” names this mathematical flux integral only; it does
not assert a physical conservation law or an entropy interpretation.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention and the spacelike slab data of
[[def-tgr-spacelike-current-slab]]. For every slice $\Sigma_t$ and every
$C^1$ current $J$ in that definition, its normal flux charge is
$$Q_J(t)=\int_\Omega wJ^0\,d^3x,$$
where $w=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}$ is the metric density in the supplied chart.

Assume the Countable Choice convention $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]] used by the smooth tangent-bundle structure in
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ with its metric-selected
connection $\nabla$, and let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart. Write
$w=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}$. Let $J$ be a $C^1$ vector field on $U$; the
connection derivative on such a field is defined by its usual chart formula
$$\nabla_bJ^a:=\partial_bJ^a+\Gamma^a{}_{cb}J^c,$$
whose coefficients are continuous. Then, throughout $U$,
$$\nabla_aJ^a=w^{-1}\partial_a(wJ^a).$$
The right-hand side is the chart expression of the scalar divergence
$\nabla_aJ^a$; no higher regularity of $J$ than $C^1$ is required.

Let $m\ge1$ and let
$$Q=\prod_{j=1}^{m}[a_j,b_j]\subseteq\mathbb R^m, \qquad a_j<b_j.$$
Then $Q$ is compact and Jordan measurable, and its boundary has Jordan
content zero. For any product $R=\prod_{j=1}^m I_j$ where each $I_j$ is one
of $[a_j,b_j]$, $(a_j,b_j)$, $[a_j,b_j)$ or $(a_j,b_j]$, the set $R$ is a
bounded Jordan set with closure contained in $Q$. Every continuous
$f:Q\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable over $R$. When $m\ge2$, each closed
coordinate face of $Q$ is compact and Jordan measurable in its own
$(m-1)$-dimensional coordinate space; the same endpoint-variant and
integrability conclusions hold for products in that face.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}$ be a bounded Jordan set and let $g:E\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Suppose that for all $x$ outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, the section $E_x$ is Jordan measurable and $g_x$ is integrable over it. Put $h(x)=\int_{E_x}g_x$ there and assign arbitrary bounded values to $h$ on $N$, with empty-section integral equal to $0$. Then $h$ is integrable on any rectangle containing the projection of $E$, its integral is independent of that rectangle and of the values on $N$, and
$$\int_Eg=\int h(x)\,dx.$$
The symmetric assertion holds for the other coordinate block.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $M$ carry an orientation in the
sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]] (so that its
charts that are oriented in that orientation have orientation-preserving
transition maps), and let $\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection. This item
fixes the metric volume form, the flux of a current through oriented $3$-faces
and finite-chain charges. The orientation of $M$ is an independent datum: it is
not determined by the metric and not by the time orientation.

**(a) Metric volume density and volume form.** Let $(U,x)$ be an oriented
chart, with metric components $g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (a)). Define the **metric volume
density**

$$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}>0\qquad\text{on }U,$$

a strictly positive smooth function because $g_{ab}$ is smooth and
$g_p$ is nondegenerate. In the chart define the local $4$-form

$$\mathrm{vol}_{g,U}:=w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3,$$

with the exterior product of [[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]] and the
coordinate covector fields of
[[prop-local-coordinate-expression-for-a-differential-form]]. That these local
forms agree on chart overlaps and therefore define one smooth nowhere-vanishing

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by

also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction

A **current** here is a $C^1$ vector field $J=J^a\partial_a$ on an open
neighborhood of $x^{-1}(\overline K)$; equivalently, its coordinate components $J^a$
are $C^1$. Its current three-form is the pointwise contraction
$\omega_J:=\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$, where
$(\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g)(X_1,X_2,X_3):=
\mathrm{vol}_g(J,X_1,X_2,X_3)$. In coordinates,
$$\omega_J=w\bigl(J^0dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3 -J^1dx^0\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3 +J^2dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^3 -J^3dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\bigr).$$
The slice orientation is chosen so that the future unit normal precedes a
positive slice basis. Since $n^0=1/\alpha>0$ and the spacetime chart is
positive, this slice orientation is $dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$; the
pullback of $\omega_J$ to $\Sigma_t$ is $wJ^0dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.
Define its signed **slice charge** (the normal flux through the spacelike
slice) by
$$Q_J(t):=\int_\Omega -g(J,n)\,dV_h.$$
Every displayed integral is the Riemann integral over the indicated bounded
Jordan set, as defined in
[[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]. The current and metric extend
continuously to the compact coordinate closure, and
[[lem-tgr-coordinate-boxes-are-compact-jordan]] proves that the open spatial
and mixed-endpoint rectangles are Jordan measurable and that these continuous
densities are Riemann integrable there.

Let $B$ denote the union of the six side faces of $K$, with outward boundary
orientation; each face is integrated over its relative interior, a bounded
Jordan rectangle whose closure is compact. The upper $x^i$ face has induced orientation
$(-1)^i dx^0\wedge\cdots\widehat{dx^i}\cdots\wedge dx^3$; the lower face
has its opposite. Thus the $i$th current-three-form pullback integrates to
the upper-minus-lower $wJ^i$ coordinate expression below. Define the
**net outward side flux** $\Phi_J(B)$ as the sum over
the three spatial coordinate directions of upper-face flux minus lower-face
flux. More explicitly, for $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ let $\Omega_i$ be the product
Jordan rectangle in the three coordinates other than $x^i$, with endpoint
convention $x^0\in[t_0,t_1]$ and $x^j\in(a_j,b_j)$ for $j\ne i$; then
$$\Phi_J(B):=\sum_{i=1}^3\int_{\Omega_i} \left. wJ^i\right|_{x^i=b_i}-\left. wJ^i\right|_{x^i=a_i}\,d^3x_{\widehat i}.$$
The integrals use the standard increasing-coordinate order on each face. For
a $C^1$ current the three-form coefficients are continuous, so the displayed
rectangular integrals exist. This extends the smooth-current flux convention
of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (b) to the present
finite coordinate faces. No unit normal to a side face is part of this
definition; in particular the flux form remains defined if a side face is
null. The term “charge” names this mathematical flux integral only; it does
not assert a physical conservation law or an entropy interpretation.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ background of
[[def-tgr-spacelike-current-slab]]. Let $K$, $\Sigma_t$, the $C^1$ current
$J$, its slice charge $Q_J(t)$ and its net outward side flux $\Phi_J(B)$ be
as in [[def-tgr-spacelike-current-slab]]. Use the oriented metric volume form
of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (a). Put
$\Pi:=\nabla_aJ^a$, using the $C^1$ divergence of
[[lem-tgr-c1-current-density-divergence]]. Then the exact finite-slab balance
is
$$Q_J(t_1)-Q_J(t_0)+\Phi_J(B)=\int_K\Pi\,\mathrm{vol}_g.$$
Here the four-volume integral is the Riemann integral on the bounded Jordan
slab $K$, whose compact closure is the supplied coordinate box. If
$\Pi\ge0$ everywhere on $K$, then
$Q_J(t_1)+\Phi_J(B)\ge Q_J(t_0)$. In particular, nonnegative local
production implies $Q_J(t_1)\ge Q_J(t_0)$ when the **net outward side flux**
is zero. If $\Pi=0$, the identity instead reads
$Q_J(t_1)-Q_J(t_0)=-\Phi_J(B)$, so zero production alone does not imply
constant slice charge.

Let $m\ge1$ and let
$$Q=\prod_{j=1}^{m}[a_j,b_j]\subseteq\mathbb R^m, \qquad a_j<b_j.$$
Then $Q$ is compact and Jordan measurable, and its boundary has Jordan
content zero. For any product $R=\prod_{j=1}^m I_j$ where each $I_j$ is one
of $[a_j,b_j]$, $(a_j,b_j)$, $[a_j,b_j)$ or $(a_j,b_j]$, the set $R$ is a
bounded Jordan set with closure contained in $Q$. Every continuous
$f:Q\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable over $R$. When $m\ge2$, each closed
coordinate face of $Q$ is compact and Jordan measurable in its own
$(m-1)$-dimensional coordinate space; the same endpoint-variant and
integrability conclusions hold for products in that face.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}$ be a bounded Jordan set and let $g:E\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Suppose that for all $x$ outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, the section $E_x$ is Jordan measurable and $g_x$ is integrable over it. Put $h(x)=\int_{E_x}g_x$ there and assign arbitrary bounded values to $h$ on $N$, with empty-section integral equal to $0$. Then $h$ is integrable on any rectangle containing the projection of $E$, its integral is independent of that rectangle and of the values on $N$, and
$$\int_Eg=\int h(x)\,dx.$$
The symmetric assertion holds for the other coordinate block.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

An orientation of an $n$-manifold is a smooth choice of a ray in $\det T_pM$ for every $p$. For $n>0$, a chart is oriented when its coordinate frame is in that ray. For $n=0$, the datum is a sign at each point; the unique empty frame does not encode both choices.

derivations.claim: Let $M=\mathbb R^4$ with coordinates $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and future direction $\partial_0$. Let $\Omega=(0,L)\times(0,L_2)\times(0,L_3)$ and $K=[0,T]\times\Omega$, with compact closure $\overline K=[0,T]\times[0,L]\times[0,L_2]\times[0,L_3]$. Define the constant vector $u=(\gamma,\gamma\beta,0,0)$ and scalar $s=s_0[1+a(x^1-\beta x^0)]$. Since $0<\beta<1$ and $aT<1$, $1+a(x^1-\beta x^0)\ge1-a\beta T>0$ on $\overline K$, so $s$ is positive there and extends smoothly to a neighborhood of $\overline K$. Also $\eta(u,u)=-\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=-1$ and $u$ is future-directed.

Put $J=su$, so $J^0=\gamma s$ and $J^1=\gamma\beta s$. In this chart $w=1$, and [F2] gives $$\nabla_aJ^a=\partial_0J^0+\partial_1J^1 =\gamma(-s_0a\beta)+\gamma\beta(s_0a)=0$$ throughout the slab; the remaining components vanish. Thus local production is zero everywhere.

By [F3] and [F5], integration of the affine density on the product rectangle gives $$Q_J(t)=\gamma s_0LL_2L_3\left(1+\frac{aL}{2}-a\beta t\right),$$ so $$Q_J(T)-Q_J(0)=-\gamma s_0a\beta TLL_2L_3<0.$$ The slice charge strictly decreases.

Only the $x^1$ side faces carry flux. Their upper-minus-lower density is $J^1(t,L,x^2,x^3)-J^1(t,0,x^2,x^3)=\gamma\beta s_0aL$, independent of $t,x^2,x^3$. Therefore the **integrated** net outward side flux is $$\Phi_J(B)=\gamma s_0a\beta TLL_2L_3>0.$$ The factor $T$ is the duration of the slab. By [F4], $Q_J(T)-Q_J(0)+\Phi_J(B)=0$, in agreement with the zero production calculation. The example refutes the unrestricted monotonicity assertion and shows that the side-flux hypothesis is essential.
